set1.q: A 67-year-old woman with poorly controlled rheumatoid arthritis has anemia of chronic disease: hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL (normal 12.0-15.5 g/dL), ferritin 260 ng/mL (normal 15-200 ng/mL) and total iron-binding capacity 220 mcg/dL (normal 250-450 mcg/dL). Which step matters most for her anemia?
opts: Referral to hematology is not usually needed in anemia of chronic disease. Tell: the anemia follows the arthritis, so controlling the arthritis is the priority.

Correct. Treating the underlying condition is the most important treatment for anemia of chronic disease; her rheumatoid arthritis is poorly controlled, and its inflammation drives the hepcidin rise and the erythropoietin suppression behind her anemia.

Erythropoietin supplementation may help in anemia of chronic disease, but its indication is a hemoglobin below 10 g/dL; hers is 10.6 g/dL. Tell: treat the inflammation first, and her hemoglobin is above the erythropoietin cut-off anyway.
ruled out by a stated finding

Her ferritin of 260 ng/mL is high, as expected in chronic disease, and gives no sign of coexistent iron deficiency (below 30 ng/mL). Tell: inflammation blocks iron through hepcidin, so extra oral iron does not fix the cause.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 31-year-old woman has iron deficiency anemia from heavy menstrual bleeding; workup finds no other source. Her hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL (normal 12.0-15.5 g/dL). She is starting oral iron and does not wish to become pregnant. Which added measure addresses the cause of her iron loss?
opts: Correct. Treatment of iron deficiency starts by treating the underlying cause. For menstrual blood loss an oral contraceptive can be given, and a continuous-cycle contraceptive should be considered, while iron is replaced. Her loss is menstrual and she wants contraception.

Parenteral iron replaces iron when oral iron is not tolerated or fails; it does nothing about the menstrual loss. She is only just starting oral iron. Tell: the question asks for the cause of the loss, not another route for iron.

Erythropoietin supplementation may help selected patients with anemia of chronic disease and a hemoglobin below 10 g/dL; it does not address menstrual iron loss. Tell: her problem is bleeding, so the fix is a contraceptive.

Colonoscopy and endoscopy evaluate a gastrointestinal bleed for colorectal cancer; her workup found no other source than menses. Tell: a gut evaluation is for gut bleeding, while menstrual loss is treated with a contraceptive.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 74-year-old man with myelodysplastic syndrome has ring sideroblasts (iron-containing mitochondria ringing the nucleus) on his marrow and needs regular red cell transfusions; his hemoglobin before each one is about 7.6 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL). Which agent was recently approved for this setting?
opts: Correct. Luspatercept is a new agent recently approved for myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts, his diagnosis. Myelodysplastic syndrome is the usual association of acquired sideroblastic anemia, and his transfusion support also warrants hematology involvement.

Sideroblastic anemia typically does not respond well to recombinant erythropoietin; epoetin alfa fits anemia of chronic disease with a hemoglobin below 10 g/dL. Tell: the agent approved for myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts is luspatercept.
Succimer chelates lead in severe lead poisoning with neurologic effects; he has myelodysplastic syndrome, not lead exposure. Tell: chelation answers lead, not a marrow disorder.
Ferrous sulfate replaces iron in iron deficiency; sideroblastic anemia already has excess total body iron, and regular transfusions add more. Tell: iron is the wrong direction here.

opts: Pallor reflects the chronic anemia of the disease, with a hematocrit usually 15 to 30 percent. Tell: urgent care is for fever, chest pain or a new neurologic deficit.
Dark urine after fava beans is the trigger story of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. Tell: her red flags are fever, chest pain and neurologic changes.

Correct. Red flags in sickle cell disease are fever, chest pain or hypoxemia, and a new neurologic deficit, each requiring urgent assessment. Education includes vaccines, fever and chest pain precautions and hematology follow-up.
Anemia is almost universal in sickle cell disease, so mild fatigue alone is expected rather than a red flag. Tell: the urgent symptoms are fever, chest pain or hypoxemia and new neurologic deficits.

set1.q: A 55-year-old woman has a hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL (normal 12.0-15.5 g/dL), mean corpuscular volume 79 fL (normal 80-100 fL), a dimorphic smear with microcytic, normal and macrocytic cells, serum iron 210 mcg/dL (normal 60-170 mcg/dL), transferrin saturation 62% (normal 20-50%) and ferritin 540 ng/mL (normal 15-200 ng/mL). Which test shows the defining feature of her likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A dimorphic smear with excess total body iron (high serum iron, transferrin saturation and ferritin) suggests sideroblastic anemia. Its defining feature is ring sideroblasts on a bone marrow aspirate: iron-containing mitochondria form a basophilic ring around the nucleus.

A stool guaiac test looks for gastrointestinal blood loss in iron deficiency; her iron values are all high, not low. Tell: overloaded iron with a dimorphic smear sends you to the marrow, not the stool.

Lead poisoning is a microcytic, hypochromic anemia with basophilic stippling, and lead can cause sideroblastic anemia, but a lead level does not show ring sideroblasts. Tell: the defining sideroblastic finding is seen only in the marrow.

C-reactive protein only shows inflammation; it cannot show ring sideroblasts, the defining feature, which a bone marrow aspirate shows. Tell: high saturation plus a dimorphic smear points to sideroblastic anemia and the marrow.

set1.q: A 52-year-old man has a hemoglobin of 10.4 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL), a white cell count of 7,200 per microliter (normal 4,500-11,000) and platelets of 240,000 per microliter (normal 150,000-450,000), with a mean corpuscular volume of 88 fL (normal 80-100 fL). Which value should be reviewed next to judge whether his bone marrow response is adequate?
opts: A bone marrow aspirate is an invasive test kept for a defined question; the first look at marrow response is a blood value. Tell: start with the reticulocyte index.

Correct. The initial approach reviews the complete blood count across all three cell lines (his white cells and platelets are normal, so there is no pancytopenia), evaluates the mean corpuscular volume (88 fL, normal), then reviews the reticulocyte index to determine whether the bone marrow response is adequate.

Serum ferritin reflects iron stores and helps once an iron problem is suspected, as with microcytosis; it does not measure marrow output. Tell: the question is whether the marrow is answering the anemia, which reticulocytes show.
The red cell distribution width measures variation in red cell volume and size, not how many new cells the marrow is releasing. Tell: size spread is not marrow response.

set1.q: A 41-year-old man has a white blood cell count of 2,800 cells per microliter (normal 4,500-11,000). His differential shows neutrophils 32% (normal 40-70%), bands 4% (normal 0-5%), lymphocytes 56% and monocytes 8%. How is his neutropenia classified?
opts: His count of 1,008 is below 1,500, the top of the mild range, so he is neutropenic. Tell: a normal-looking band count does not remove the low neutrophils from the formula.

Correct. Absolute neutrophil count = 2,800 x (32 + 4) / 100 = 1,008 cells per microliter, inside the mild range of 1,000-1,500. Using the neutrophils alone would give 896 and wrongly call it moderate.
Moderate is 500-999, which is what the neutrophils alone give (2,800 x 32% = 896). Tell: adding the 4% bands lifts the count to 1,008, which is mild.
Severe neutropenia is below 500 cells per microliter, about half of his count. Tell: 1,008 is two grades above severe.

set1.q: A 40-year-old woman with autoimmune hemolytic anemia has gone into remission on treatment. She asks what her follow-up will involve. Which follow-up plan is appropriate?
opts: Correct. Follow-up of autoimmune hemolysis is to treat the cause, monitor for relapse and thrombosis and keep hematology care. Relapse may occur, and the outcome depends on the cause and the response to treatment.

Avoiding oxidative triggers and seeking care for jaundice or dark urine is the follow-up for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. Tell: autoimmune hemolysis is followed for relapse and thrombosis.
Genetic counseling belongs to thalassemia, an inherited globin disorder. Tell: autoimmune hemolysis is acquired, so follow-up watches for relapse and clots.
Relapse may occur, so remission is not the end of follow-up. Tell: she needs monitoring for relapse and thrombosis with hematology care.

set1.q: A 60-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy has a white blood cell count of 1,800 cells per microliter (normal 4,500-11,000). Her differential shows neutrophils 20% (normal 40-70%), bands 5% (normal 0-5%), lymphocytes 65% and monocytes 10%. What is her absolute neutrophil count?
opts: 90 is the bands alone, 1,800 x 5%, without the mature neutrophils. Tell: add the neutrophil and band percentages first, 20 + 5 = 25%.
360 is the neutrophils alone, 1,800 x 20%, leaving out the bands. Tell: bands are part of the formula, so the count is 1,800 x 25% = 450.

Correct. Absolute neutrophil count = 1,800 x (20 + 5) / 100 = 450 cells per microliter, which is severe neutropenia (below 500). If she develops fever, that count makes it an emergency needing cultures and empiric antipseudomonal antibiotics.
1,170 is the lymphocyte count, 1,800 x 65%, which does not enter the absolute neutrophil count. Tell: only neutrophils and bands are counted.

set1.q: A 12-year-old girl has beta thalassemia with moderate chronic anemia, splenomegaly and jaundice. Her hemoglobin is stable at 8.5 g/dL (normal 12.0-16.0 g/dL), and she has no symptoms requiring urgent transfusion. Which supportive treatment is appropriate?
opts: Glucocorticoids treat autoimmune hemolytic anemia, which is Coombs positive; thalassemia is Coombs negative. Tell: thalassemia care is supportive, with folic acid.
Transfusion is given only when absolutely necessary because it can exacerbate iron overload, and she is stable. Tell: support her with folic acid and monitoring.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Treatment of thalassemia is supportive: transfusion only when absolutely necessary, because it can exacerbate iron overload, plus folic acid and genetic counseling. A stable girl without an urgent need gets the supportive measures.
Iron overload is already part of thalassemia's course, so adding iron would worsen it. Tell: the supplement on the thalassemia list is folic acid.

set1.q: A 63-year-old man on hemodialysis for kidney failure has iron deficiency from the iron lost at each treatment; his hemoglobin is 10.3 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL). Which iron option is designed to replace the iron lost during each hemodialysis session?
opts: Alternate-day ferrous sulfate is the preferred oral schedule for iron deficiency in general, but it is not built to replace the iron lost with each dialysis session. Tell: the dialysis-specific option is added to the dialysate.
Oral pyridoxine is not an iron preparation, so it cannot replace the iron lost during each hemodialysis treatment. Tell: replacing iron lost during dialysis takes an iron product in the dialysate.

Succimer chelation therapy is not an iron preparation and puts no iron back. Tell: the product designed to replace the iron lost during each hemodialysis treatment is ferric pyrophosphate citrate, added to the dialysate.

Correct. Ferric pyrophosphate citrate is an approved additive to the dialysate, designed to replace the iron that is lost during each hemodialysis treatment. It delivers iron through the dialysis circuit itself.

set1.q: A 26-year-old man with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency develops a urinary tract infection while traveling. He has a supply of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole from a previous prescription and asks whether he may take it. What is the best response?
opts: Males are the ones generally affected because the disorder is X-linked recessive. Tell: he is exactly the patient at risk, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a common trigger.

Correct. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is on the list of common triggers of acute hemolytic anemia in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, with nitrofurantoin, quinolones and phenazopyridine. His infection needs an antibiotic that is not one of these oxidant triggers.
Hydration treats an attack once it happens; it does not make an oxidant trigger safe to take. Tell: the drug itself is on the trigger list, so he should not take it.
A shorter course is still an exposure to a drug with high oxidative potential, and hemolysis follows after a lag of 2 to 3 days. Tell: triggers are avoided, not shortened.

set1.q: A 39-year-old man has autoimmune hemolytic anemia with a positive direct antiglobulin test. He is stable with hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL), and secondary causes have been ruled out. Which is the initial treatment?
opts: Hydroxyurea is not among the treatments listed for autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Tell: an antibody-mediated hemolysis is treated with glucocorticoids first.

Correct. With secondary causes ruled out and no instability, autoimmune hemolytic anemia is treated with glucocorticoids initially. Rituximab is the other named agent, and immunosuppressants or splenectomy are further options.
Rituximab is a named treatment but follows glucocorticoids, which are given initially. Tell: start with steroids; the antibody drug comes next.
Splenectomy sits among the other options after medical therapy. Tell: a stable first presentation begins with glucocorticoids.

set1.q: A 38-year-old woman has fatigue, dark urine and yellow eyes. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL (normal 12.0-16.0 g/dL), reticulocytes 6% (normal 0.5-2.5%), haptoglobin undetectable (normal 30-200 mg/dL), lactate dehydrogenase 610 U/L (normal 140-280 U/L), and the urinalysis shows hemoglobin. Which pattern of red cell destruction do these results indicate?
opts: A production failure would give a low reticulocyte count. Tell: her reticulocytes are 6 percent, a marrow working hard to replace destroyed cells.
ruled out by a stated finding

Iron deficiency is a production anemia from chronic blood loss and does not consume haptoglobin or spill hemoglobin into the urine. Tell: lysis markers, a high lactate dehydrogenase and absent haptoglobin, point to destruction.

Yellow eyes alone could suggest a bile problem, but obstruction does not explain anemia with high reticulocytes, absent haptoglobin and urine hemoglobin. Tell: those findings describe red cells breaking open inside the vessels.

Correct. In intravascular hemolysis free hemoglobin is picked up by haptoglobin and carried to the liver, so haptoglobin becomes decreased or absent, and because that binding is incomplete some hemoglobin reaches the urine. Her undetectable haptoglobin and urine hemoglobin fit, with a high reticulocyte count and lactate dehydrogenase from cell lysis.

set1.q: A 5-month-old boy who missed newborn screening is brought in with poor weight gain, pallor and painful swelling of both hands and feet. Hemoglobin analysis confirms sickle cell disease. His mother asks why he was well until now. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Correct. Infants who bypass newborn screening usually present within the first two years of life, and symptoms usually start around 5 months with the transition from fetal hemoglobin (HbF) to HbS. Swelling of the extremities comes from vaso-occlusion, with failure to thrive, pain, anemia and splenomegaly.
Sickle cell disease presents in infancy and early childhood, usually within the first two years of life. Tell: the timing turns on the switch from HbF to HbS around 5 months.
Infections are a manifestation of sickle cell disease, not its cause; the disease is an inherited beta globin mutation. Tell: symptoms appear as protective HbF gives way to HbS.
Breast milk is not named as protective. Tell: his early protection was his own fetal hemoglobin, and symptoms begin around 5 months as HbS takes over.

set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and gastroesophageal reflux takes metformin, amlodipine, atorvastatin and omeprazole. She has a mean corpuscular volume of 107 fL (normal 80-100 fL), hypersegmented neutrophils, a low folate level and a normal B12 level. Which of her medications is listed as a cause of folate deficiency?
opts: Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, and proton pump inhibitors are listed as a medication cause of iron deficiency anemia, which is microcytic. Tell: her cells are large and her folate is low, which points to metformin.

Amlodipine is not on the list of drugs that cause folate deficiency (methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil, hydroxyurea, phenytoin, metformin). Tell: of her medications, only the diabetes drug is on that list.

Atorvastatin does not appear among the drug causes of folate deficiency. Tell: the listed drugs are methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil, hydroxyurea, phenytoin and metformin, and metformin is the one she takes.

Correct. Metformin is on the list of drugs that cause folate deficiency, with methotrexate, 5-fluorouracil, hydroxyurea and phenytoin. Her low folate with a megaloblastic picture and a normal B12 fits that drug cause.

set1.q: A 41-year-old woman has taken oral iron for iron deficiency anemia for 2 months. Her hemoglobin is now 13.2 g/dL (normal 12.0-15.5 g/dL) and her mean corpuscular volume 86 fL (normal 80-100 fL). She asks whether she can stop the iron. What should she be told?
opts: Stop now that values are normal
Normal blood counts mean the circulating deficit is corrected, but the stores are still empty. Tell: iron continues for 3-6 months after normalization.
Two weeks is too short to refill iron stores; the recommended extension is 3-6 months after values normalize. Tell: the tail of therapy is measured in months.
Continue for the rest of her life
Lifelong iron is not the plan once the cause is treated; therapy continues 3-6 months after normalization to replenish stores and then ends. Tell: a set extension, not indefinite therapy.
Correct. Her values are back to normal at 2 months, the expected timing. Iron therapy should continue for 3-6 months after normal hematologic values are restored, to replenish iron stores.

set1.q: A 31-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has 2 weeks of fatigue and jaundice. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL (normal 12.0-16.0 g/dL), reticulocytes 8% (normal 0.5-2.5%), and haptoglobin is low (normal 30-200 mg/dL). Which test will show whether her red cells are coated with IgG or complement?
opts: Correct. Lupus is a common secondary cause of autoimmune hemolytic anemia. In the direct antiglobulin, or Coombs, test her washed red cells are combined with Coombs reagent, which binds only cells coated with IgG or complement; a positive test cross-links and agglutinates them.

Electrophoresis analyzes the globin chains in thalassemia and hemoglobinopathies, which are Coombs negative. Tell: her lupus points to an antibody, which only the antiglobulin test can show on the cell.
A glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase level confirms an enzyme deficiency about 8 weeks after an attack. Tell: she has an autoimmune disease and needs a test for antibody on her red cells.
An iron panel answers deficiency or overload questions, not whether antibody coats the red cells. Tell: hemolysis with lupus calls for the Coombs test.

set1.q: A 67-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease has fatigue. Hemoglobin is 9.4 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL), mean corpuscular volume 88 fL (normal 80-100 fL), reticulocyte count low, ferritin 280 ng/mL (normal 30-300 ng/mL) and transferrin saturation 14% (normal 20-50%). Which treatment step does his iron panel call for?
opts: No iron, since ferritin is normal

His normal ferritin does not clear him: a low transferrin saturation may indicate iron-restricted erythropoiesis despite normal or high ferritin. Tell: in kidney disease the saturation of 14% may indicate iron-restricted erythropoiesis.
Nothing in his counts points to a folate problem. Tell: his mean corpuscular volume of 88 fL is normal and his iron panel shows restricted iron, so folate is not the missing piece.

Nothing in his counts or history points to a marrow failure that a biopsy would need to show. Tell: his anemia has a clear kidney explanation and a correctable iron restriction, so a marrow biopsy is not the next treatment step.

Correct. In anemia of chronic kidney disease a low transferrin saturation may indicate iron-restricted erythropoiesis despite a normal or high ferritin, because inflammation and hepcidin restrict available iron. The treatment step is to correct the iron deficiency, with oral or intravenous iron, and to consider an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent by stage, hemoglobin and risk.

set1.q: A 36-year-old man takes isoniazid for latent tuberculosis, lisinopril for hypertension, atorvastatin for high cholesterol and omeprazole for reflux. His hemoglobin is 9.5 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL), and a bone marrow aspirate shows ring sideroblasts (iron-containing mitochondria forming a ring around the nucleus). Which medication should be stopped?
opts: Atorvastatin is not a listed cause of sideroblastic anemia; the drugs named are isoniazid and chlorambucil. Tell: look for the antituberculosis drug when ring sideroblasts appear.

Correct. Ring sideroblasts define sideroblastic anemia, and isoniazid is one of the drugs behind its acquired, reversible type (with chlorambucil, alcohol, copper deficiency, hypothermia and lead). Treatment begins by removing the offending agent.

Omeprazole is not a listed cause of sideroblastic anemia; the drugs named for the acquired, reversible type are isoniazid and chlorambucil. Tell: ring sideroblasts point to isoniazid, not to acid suppression.

Lisinopril is not among the reversible causes of sideroblastic anemia (alcohol, isoniazid, chlorambucil, copper deficiency, hypothermia, lead poisoning). Tell: the antituberculosis drug is the offender.

set1.q: A 44-year-old man has fatigue and his brother has hemochromatosis. His iron panel shows ferritin 180 micrograms/L (normal 12-300 micrograms/L) and transferrin saturation 32% (normal 20-50%), and he has no infection or inflammatory illness. How should this panel be classified?
opts: Both of his values are under the cut-offs, ferritin under 300 micrograms/L and saturation under 45 percent, which is the definition of no overload. Tell: overload is only in play when a value crosses its cut-off.
Secondary hemochromatosis is iron accumulation, such as from parenteral iron overload, and still requires overload. Tell: his panel shows no overload at all.
ruled out by a stated finding
His ferritin of 180 micrograms/L and saturation of 32 percent are within their normal ranges, not low. Tell: the panel is read against the overload cut-offs, and both are below them.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. If ferritin is less than 300 micrograms/L and transferrin saturation is less than 45 percent, there is no iron overload. His ferritin of 180 and saturation of 32 percent are both below the cut-offs, and with no inflammatory illness the acute phase caution does not apply.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with B12 deficiency had months of numbness in her hands and feet and an unsteady gait before she was diagnosed. She has now started B12 replacement. She asks whether her numbness will go away. Which response is accurate?
opts: It may or may not improve

Correct. Neurologic findings of B12 deficiency may or may not improve with B12 supplementation; the blood counts improve, but delayed B12 treatment may leave deficits, so her neurologic recovery is monitored. Her months of untreated symptoms make a lasting deficit possible.
Prompt, certain resolution is not what to expect: neurologic findings may or may not improve with B12. Tell: her counts will recover reliably, but nerve damage after a delayed diagnosis may persist.
It will improve once folate is added
Folate does not repair B12 neuropathy, and folate without B12 can let permanent neurologic symptoms worsen. Tell: her nerves depend on B12, and even then recovery may or may not occur.
B12 is the treatment that may help her nerves; it does not worsen them. Tell: what may worsen neurologic symptoms is folate given without evaluating B12.

set1.q: An 81-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease, on several medications, is found to have a new anemia on routine labs. Which approach is listed for elderly patients with a cytopenia?
opts: Newborn screens are the infant priority. Tell: her age calls for the elderly checklist, including her medications and kidney disease.
The elderly row says to tailor treatment to function, comorbidities and goals, not to apply it uniformly. Tell: work up iron, B12, kidney disease, drugs and marrow, then tailor.

Correct. In the elderly, check iron and B12 deficiency, chronic kidney disease, drugs and marrow disorders such as myelodysplastic syndrome, then tailor treatment to function, comorbidities and goals. Her kidney disease and medication list are both on that checklist.
Heavy menses is the adolescent priority. Tell: an older woman is checked for iron and B12 deficiency, kidney disease, drugs and marrow disorders.

set1.q: A 4-year-old boy with known glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency develops abdominal pain, jaundice and dark urine 2 days after he was found playing in a closet where mothballs were stored. Which exposure is the likely trigger?
opts: Fava beans are a classic dietary trigger, but his exposure was the closet where mothballs were stored. Tell: mothballs mean naphthalene.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Naphthalene in mothballs is a listed trigger of acute hemolytic anemia in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. The 2-day lag, abdominal pain, jaundice and dark urine match drug- or toxin-induced hemolysis after oxidative stress.
Nothing in his story points to lead exposure, and his acute hemolysis came 2 days after an exposure in a known enzyme deficiency. Tell: mothballs contain naphthalene, a listed trigger.

Nothing in his story points to copper exposure, while the stored mothballs do point to an oxidant trigger. Tell: the stored mothballs point to naphthalene, an oxidant trigger in his enzyme deficiency.

set1.q: A 39-year-old woman started ferrous sulfate two weeks ago for iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL, normal 12.0-15.5 g/dL) and now has hard, infrequent stools. She wants to keep taking the iron. Which advice is most appropriate?
opts: Parenteral iron is for patients intolerant of or refractory to oral iron; she has a manageable side effect and wants to continue. Tell: treat the constipation before abandoning the oral route.
Stopping iron leaves her anemia untreated, when the expected side effect has a simple remedy. Tell: oral iron is given with a laxative or stool softener so it can continue.
Add a laxative or stool softener

Correct. Gastrointestinal side effects of ferrous sulfate are common, nausea and especially constipation, so it is given with at least an as-needed laxative or stool softener. She wants to continue, and treating the constipation keeps her adherent.
Antacids (calcium) are a dietary cause of iron deficiency because they impair iron, and they do not treat constipation. Tell: her side effect is constipation, so the partner is a stool softener.

set1.q: A 35-year-old woman has a hemoglobin of 9.9 g/dL (normal 12.0-15.5 g/dL), mean corpuscular volume 73 fL (normal 80-100 fL), ferritin 7 ng/mL (normal 15-200 ng/mL), total iron-binding capacity 470 mcg/dL (normal 250-450 mcg/dL) and transferrin saturation 6% (normal 20-50%). She has no inflammatory illness. Which anemia do these iron studies fit?
opts: Correct. Her iron panel is the iron deficiency pattern: reduced ferritin (7 ng/mL), reduced transferrin saturation (6%) and increased total iron-binding capacity (470 mcg/dL), with microcytosis (mean corpuscular volume below 80 fL). With no inflammation, a low ferritin is reliable.

Anemia of chronic disease has a normal or increased ferritin and a decreased total iron-binding capacity; hers are 7 ng/mL and 470 mcg/dL, and she has no inflammatory illness. Tell: low ferritin with high binding capacity rules chronic disease out.
ruled out by a stated finding

Her iron studies match the iron deficiency pattern: reduced ferritin (7 ng/mL), reduced transferrin saturation (6%) and increased total iron-binding capacity (470 mcg/dL). Tell: low ferritin with a high binding capacity is iron deficiency, not sideroblastic anemia.

Thalassemia gives a greater degree of microcytosis for its hemoglobin and a normal or elevated red cell count; it does not deplete ferritin. Tell: a ferritin of 7 ng/mL with a high binding capacity is an iron problem, not a globin problem.

set1.q: A 44-year-old man with inflammatory bowel disease has a hemoglobin of 10.0 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL), mean corpuscular volume 76 fL (normal 80-100 fL) and a C-reactive protein of 4.8 mg/dL (normal below 1.0 mg/dL). His ferritin is 21 ng/mL (normal 15-200 ng/mL). How should his iron status be classified?
opts: Iron overload would show a high ferritin; his ferritin is 21 ng/mL, under the 30 ng/mL line that signals coexistent iron deficiency. Tell: overload needs a high ferritin.

Correct. In anemia of chronic disease serum ferritin should be normal or increased; a value below 30 ng/mL indicates coexistent iron deficiency. His ferritin of 21 ng/mL sits inside the reference range yet below 30 ng/mL, despite active inflammation that would push ferritin up.
Chronic disease alone; ferritin is normal

His ferritin is within the lab range, but in chronic disease the cut-off that matters is 30 ng/mL, and 21 ng/mL is under it. Tell: inflammation should hold ferritin up, so a value below 30 ng/mL means iron deficiency too.
ruled out by a stated finding

Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so with a C-reactive protein of 4.8 mg/dL it should be normal or high; a value of 21 ng/mL is low for this setting. Tell: below 30 ng/mL in chronic disease means stores are short.

set1.q: A 7-year-old boy with sickle cell disease suddenly develops weakness of his right arm and slurred speech at school. He is afebrile. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Routine hematology follow-up is part of long-term care but too slow for a new neurologic deficit. Tell: red flags need urgent assessment today.
Penicillin prophylaxis prevents infection with encapsulated bacteria and does nothing for an acute neurologic event. Tell: a new deficit is a red flag for urgent assessment.

Correct. A new neurologic deficit is a red flag in sickle cell disease requiring urgent assessment, as are fever and chest pain with hypoxemia. Stroke is a pediatric complication, about 300 times more common than in unaffected children.
Fluids at home do not address a red flag; a new neurologic deficit requires urgent assessment. Tell: arm weakness and slurred speech in a child with sickle cell disease suggest stroke.

set1.q: A 19-year-old woman has fatigue, recurrent infections and easy bruising. Her complete blood count shows pancytopenia, the reticulocyte count is low, and the peripheral smear shows no abnormal cells. Which test is required to make the diagnosis?
opts: Repeating the complete blood count with differential documents the trend of a cytopenia, but her pancytopenia is already established. Tell: the count shows that all three lines are low; only the marrow shows why.
Methylmalonic acid separates B12 from folate deficiency in a macrocytic anemia. Tell: her smear shows no megaloblastic change, and pancytopenia from stem cell loss is diagnosed in the marrow.

Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies support pernicious anemia, the most frequent cause of B12 deficiency. Tell: she has pancytopenia with a normal smear, not a megaloblastic anemia, so the marrow must be sampled.

Correct. Pancytopenia in a young woman with infections and bruising raises aplastic anemia, and a bone marrow biopsy is required for the diagnosis and to exclude other causes. Urgent or emergent consultation with a hematologist/oncologist is indicated.

set1.q: A 27-year-old man has 1 week of fatigue and mild scleral icterus. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL) with reticulocytes 5% (normal 0.5-2.5%), and hemolytic anemia is suspected. Which bilirubin result is expected?
opts: Clinical jaundice appears when total bilirubin exceeds 2.0 mg/dL (normal 0.3-1.2 mg/dL), so his visible icterus means the total is raised. Tell: yellow sclerae are themselves a bilirubin result.
ruled out by a stated finding
The unconjugated fraction rises in hemolysis because macrophages release it from destroyed red cells. Tell: in hemolysis the unconjugated fraction is the one that climbs most.

Correct. In hemolytic anemia both bilirubin fractions are likely elevated, with unconjugated greater than conjugated, because macrophages destroying red cells release unconjugated bilirubin that the liver conjugates afterward. His icterus and high reticulocytes fit a hemolytic source upstream of the liver.

A conjugated-predominant rise points after the liver has done its work, not to red cell breakdown. Tell: hemolysis delivers unconjugated bilirubin to the liver faster than it can be conjugated, so unconjugated leads.

set2.q: A 52-year-old woman has fatigue and dark urine. Hemoglobin is 8.8 g/dL (normal 12.0-16.0 g/dL), reticulocytes 6% (normal 0.5-2.5%), and her peripheral smear shows many schistocytes (red blood cell fragments). Which process is most likely?
opts: The hallmark finding of hemolysis is the presence of schistocytes, red blood cell fragments, and her smear shows many; nothing here points to sideroblastic anemia. Tell: her smear shows broken circulating red cells, the hallmark of hemolysis.
Aplastic anemia is marrow failure and would bring a low reticulocyte count. Tell: her reticulocytes are high and her smear shows fragments, so cells are being destroyed, not under-produced.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Schistocytes, red blood cell fragments, are the hallmark finding of hemolysis on the peripheral smear. Her anemia with a high reticulocyte count and dark urine fits premature destruction of red cells with a compensating marrow.

Her smear shows many schistocytes, and the hallmark finding of hemolysis is the presence of schistocytes; her high reticulocyte count also prompts consideration of hemolysis, not megaloblastic anemia. Tell: fragmented red cells mean destruction.

set2.q: A 46-year-old woman with autoimmune hemolytic anemia arrives confused, with heart rate 128/min and blood pressure 82/50 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 5.2 g/dL (normal 12.0-16.0 g/dL), down from 7.9 g/dL 2 days ago. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. Immediate stabilization is considered when hemoglobin is below 6 g/dL, falls rapidly or the patient is unstable, and she has all three. Contact the blood bank early.
Glucocorticoids are the initial disease treatment, but she is hypotensive and confused with a hemoglobin of 5.2 g/dL. Tell: instability comes first, stabilization and the blood bank.
Splenectomy does not address her unstable state right now. Tell: a hemoglobin below 6 g/dL with instability needs immediate stabilization and blood bank contact.
Waiting ignores a hemoglobin under 6 g/dL that fell 2.7 g/dL in 2 days in an unstable patient. Tell: any of those three findings is a reason to consider immediate stabilization.

set2.q: A 24-year-old man with known glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency has 2 days of dysuria and urinary frequency, and his urinalysis confirms a urinary tract infection. Which of these medications should be avoided?
opts: Hydration is part of the treatment of a hemolytic attack in this enzyme deficiency, not a trigger. Tell: the danger lies in the oxidant drugs on the trigger list, such as nitrofurantoin.
Amoxicillin does not appear on the list of common triggers. Tell: of these choices, only nitrofurantoin is a listed oxidant trigger for hemolysis.

Correct. Nitrofurantoin is on the list of common triggers of acute hemolytic anemia in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, quinolones and phenazopyridine. His urinary tract infection needs an agent that is not an oxidant trigger.

Cephalexin is not on the list of common triggers, which names nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, quinolones and phenazopyridine among the urinary drugs. Tell: the drug to avoid here is the listed oxidant, nitrofurantoin.

set2.q: A 74-year-old man with atrial fibrillation takes apixaban. He has fatigue and dark stools; hemoglobin is 6.9 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL), mean corpuscular volume 68 fL (normal 80-100 fL) and ferritin 4 ng/mL (normal 15-200 ng/mL). Besides a gastrointestinal consult, what should be done about his anticoagulant?
opts: Correct. His microcytic anemia with a very low ferritin is severe iron deficiency, likely from gastrointestinal blood loss. Anticoagulants are discontinued when the anemia is severe, in consultation with cardiology, because his atrial fibrillation is the reason he takes one.
Continue it and start oral iron alone

Iron replacement is needed, but continuing the anticoagulant while severe iron deficiency and probable bleeding go on ignores the advice to stop it when anemia is severe. Tell: with probable ongoing bleeding, the anticoagulant is reconsidered with cardiology, not left unchanged.

Adding another antithrombotic agent to a man with dark stools and severe iron deficiency adds bleeding risk. Tell: in severe anemia the anticoagulant is stopped, with cardiology's input, not reinforced.

Erythropoietin supplementation belongs to anemia of chronic disease; his very low ferritin is iron deficiency from blood loss. Tell: the fix for severe iron deficiency on an anticoagulant is stopping the anticoagulant with cardiology and replacing iron.

set2.q: A 38-year-old man recovering from a viral illness has a white blood cell count of 3,000 cells per microliter (normal 4,500-11,000). His differential shows neutrophils 35% (normal 40-70%), bands 5% (normal 0-5%), lymphocytes 52% and monocytes 8%. What is his absolute neutrophil count?
opts: 150 is the bands alone, 3,000 x 5%, leaving out the mature neutrophils. Tell: the formula adds the neutrophil and band percentages, 35 + 5 = 40%, before multiplying.
1,050 is the neutrophils alone, 3,000 x 35%, with the bands left out. Tell: bands are added to neutrophils, so the count is 3,000 x 40% = 1,200.

Correct. Absolute neutrophil count = white count x (neutrophils + bands)% / 100 = 3,000 x (35 + 5) / 100 = 1,200 cells per microliter, which is mild neutropenia (1,000-1,500). Transient viral leukopenia often resolves after recovery.
1,560 is the lymphocyte count, 3,000 x 52%, which is not part of the absolute neutrophil count. Tell: only neutrophils and bands enter the formula.

set2.q: A 58-year-old man has a hemoglobin of 11.0 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL), mean corpuscular volume 78 fL (normal 80-100 fL), ferritin 140 ng/mL (normal 15-200 ng/mL) and total iron-binding capacity 260 mcg/dL (normal 250-450 mcg/dL). He has no known infection or autoimmune disease. Which test helps decide whether inflammation is affecting his ferritin?
opts: Fecal occult blood test and urinalysis

A fecal occult blood test and urinalysis look for a source of blood loss once iron deficiency is suspected; they do not reveal inflammation behind a normal ferritin. Tell: inflammation is measured with a sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein.
Bone marrow aspirate for ring sideroblasts

A bone marrow aspirate is not a test for inflammation behind a ferritin value; when inflammation is not clinically known, a sedimentation rate and/or C-reactive protein can help. Tell: the question is whether ferritin is an inflamed reading, which blood markers of inflammation answer.
Repeat ferritin after a month of iron

Repeating ferritin after empiric iron does not tell whether inflammation is raising it, because ferritin itself is an acute phase reactant. Tell: check the inflammation directly with a sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein.

Correct. Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so an inflammatory condition can lift it into the normal range even with iron deficiency; a normal ferritin does not exclude iron deficiency. When inflammation is not clinically known, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate and/or C-reactive protein can help.

set2.q: A 51-year-old woman has confirmed B12 deficiency with a megaloblastic anemia. Pernicious anemia is suspected. Which blood test is specific for pernicious anemia, though not sensitive?
opts: Homocysteine rises in both B12 and folate deficiency because its metabolism needs both vitamins. Tell: it cannot name the cause of her B12 deficiency; anti-intrinsic factor antibodies point to pernicious anemia.

Correct. Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune reaction against parietal cells and/or intrinsic factor. Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies can sometimes be detected in the blood and are specific but not sensitive, so a positive result supports the diagnosis while a negative one does not exclude it.
Anti-parietal cell antibodies may be present but are neither sensitive nor specific for pernicious anemia. Tell: the antibody that is specific is the one against intrinsic factor.
Methylmalonic acid confirms B12 deficiency, rising with B12 but not folate deficiency, and her deficiency is already confirmed. Tell: it proves the vitamin is low, not that the cause is autoimmune.

set2.q: A 2-year-old girl with sickle cell disease is seen for a well-child visit. Her parents ask what can prevent serious infections, since children with her disease are susceptible to encapsulated bacteria. Which preventive plan is indicated?
opts: Correct. Sickle cell disease brings increased susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria, so prevention is vaccinations, indicated childhood penicillin prophylaxis and infection education. Prevention and emergency care vary with age, genotype and clinical history.

Iron does not prevent infection, and transfusions in sickle cell disease call for monitoring of iron loading. Tell: infection prevention in a child with sickle cell disease is penicillin plus vaccines.
Vaccinations are part of prevention in sickle cell disease, not something to postpone. Tell: vaccines and penicillin prophylaxis protect against encapsulated bacteria.
Hydroxyurea raises fetal hemoglobin and reduces vaso-occlusive events but does not replace infection prevention. Tell: the prevention line names vaccines and childhood penicillin prophylaxis.

set2.q: A 7-year-old boy has pallor and fatigue; his maternal uncle had the same anemia. His hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL (normal 11.5-15.5 g/dL), and his marrow shows ring sideroblasts (iron-containing mitochondria in a ring around the nucleus). He takes no medications and has no lead exposure. Which type of sideroblastic anemia fits best?
opts: Lead poisoning is a reversible cause of sideroblastic anemia, but he has no lead exposure. Tell: an affected maternal uncle points to inheritance, usually X-linked.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Sideroblastic anemia has three types: hereditary (usually X-linked), acquired (usually myelodysplastic syndrome) and acquired reversible (alcohol, drugs, copper deficiency, hypothermia, lead). About two thirds of cases present in males in early childhood or adolescence; an affected boy with an affected maternal uncle and no exposures fits the hereditary type.

The acquired type is usually associated with myelodysplastic syndrome, a marrow disorder that would not explain an affected maternal uncle. Tell: a young boy with family history points to the hereditary, X-linked type.
Drugs such as isoniazid or chlorambucil cause the acquired, reversible type, but he takes no medications. Tell: no drug exposure plus family history means hereditary.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 50-year-old woman with a microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, normal 12.0-15.5 g/dL; mean corpuscular volume 74 fL, normal 80-100 fL) took oral iron correctly for 3 months with no rise in hemoglobin. Colonoscopy and endoscopy were normal, and her iron studies are equivocal, so the diagnosis is not confirmed. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Cardiology is consulted when an anticoagulant may need to be stopped in severe iron deficiency; no anticoagulant is mentioned. Tell: an unconfirmed diagnosis with no response to iron goes to hematology.
Diet is unlikely to explain a microcytic anemia that did not respond to 3 months of correctly taken iron. Tell: failure of oral iron with an unclear diagnosis is a hematology question.
Her colonoscopy and endoscopy were already normal; the gut consult is for a gastrointestinal bleed. Tell: the open questions are the diagnosis and the lack of response, which hematology addresses.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Referral to hematology is recommended when the diagnosis of iron deficiency is not confirmed or the patient is unresponsive to oral iron therapy. She has both: no response after 3 months of correct use and equivocal iron studies.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease has a hemoglobin of 8.9 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL) despite iron repletion, and his primary care clinician is unsure whether to begin an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Gastroenterology referral is for iron deficiency when a gastrointestinal blood loss source must be found. Tell: his iron is repleted and the open question is the erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, a nephrology decision.

Oncology joins hematology for aplastic anemia, which needs urgent consultation and a marrow biopsy. Tell: his anemia is explained by advanced kidney disease, and the referral for agent decisions is nephrology.

Correct. Nephrology referral is advised for advanced chronic kidney disease, erythropoiesis-stimulating agent decisions or uncertainty, and he has all three. Anemia of chronic kidney disease is often chronic and may improve with iron or an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent as indicated.
Hematology is the referral for aplastic anemia and for persistent or unexplained severe neutropenia. Tell: his anemia follows his kidney disease, and agent decisions belong to nephrology.

Anemia due to deficient production of red blood cells 3. Iron deficiency 4. Anemia of chronic disease 5. Sideroblastic anemia 6. Megaloblastic anemia 7. Aplastic anemia 8. Anemia due to renal failure
set2.q: A 29-year-old woman has fatigue. Her hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL (normal 12.0-15.5 g/dL), mean corpuscular volume 71 fL (normal 80-100 fL) and mean corpuscular hemoglobin 22 pg (normal 27-31 pg). How should her anemia be classified by these indices?
opts: Normocytic would need a mean corpuscular volume of 80-100 fL and normochromic a mean corpuscular hemoglobin of 27-31 pg; her 71 fL and 22 pg are both below range. Tell: two low indices mean small, pale cells.
ruled out by a stated finding
A macrocytic, normochromic anemia has a mean corpuscular volume above 100 fL, as in megaloblastic anemia; hers is 71 fL. Tell: macrocytic means big cells, and her cells are small.
Her cells are microcytic, but a mean corpuscular hemoglobin of 22 pg, below the 27-31 pg range, is hypochromic, not hyperchromic. Tell: less hemoglobin per cell means paler cells.

Correct. Her mean corpuscular volume of 71 fL is below 80 fL, which is microcytosis, and her mean corpuscular hemoglobin of 22 pg is below 27 pg, which is hypochromia (pale cells). That microcytic, hypochromic pattern is the complete blood count of iron deficiency and of its differential.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman with untreated hypothyroidism has fatigue and a hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dL (normal 12-16 g/dL). Her mean corpuscular volume is 106 fL (normal 80-100 fL). B12, folate, homocysteine and methylmalonic acid levels are normal, and the smear shows no macro-ovalocytes or hypersegmented neutrophils. How is her anemia best classified?
opts: Megaloblastic anemia is macrocytosis with macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils from B12 or folate deficiency. Tell: her smear lacks both features and her vitamin and metabolite levels are normal.
ruled out by a stated finding
A microcytic anemia has a mean corpuscular volume below 80 fL, as in iron deficiency or lead poisoning. Tell: her volume is 106 fL, above the normal range, so it is macrocytic.
A normocytic anemia keeps the mean corpuscular volume within 80-100 fL, as in anemia of chronic kidney disease. Tell: her 106 fL is above 100, which defines macrocytosis.

Correct. A mean corpuscular volume above 100 fL makes her anemia macrocytic, and normal B12, folate and metabolite levels with no megaloblastic smear changes make it non-megaloblastic. Hypothyroidism is a listed non-megaloblastic cause, and such causes usually keep the volume below 115 fL, as hers is.

set2.q: A 28-year-old woman with iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, normal 12.0-15.5 g/dL) asks how to take her liquid ferrous sulfate so that she absorbs it best with the fewest side effects. Which instruction is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. The better-absorbed oral preparation is taken in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of orange juice: its low pH, citric acid and vitamin C help uptake and reduce exposure of free iron to the rest of the gut, limiting side effects.
With a meal and a glass of milk

Taking ferrous sulfate with food reduces side effects but also decreases absorption, and calcium works against iron too. Tell: the instruction that helps both absorption and side effects is an empty stomach with orange juice.
At bedtime with an antacid tablet
Antacids (calcium) are a dietary cause of iron deficiency, so taking iron with one undermines absorption. Tell: the preferred partner is acidic orange juice, in the morning.
With breakfast and a cup of tea
Tea drinking is a dietary factor behind iron deficiency, and food lowers absorption. Tell: swap the tea and meal for an empty stomach and a full glass of orange juice.

opts: Methylene blue is a listed trigger of hemolysis in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and is not a sickle cell therapy. Tell: disease modification is hydroxyurea.
Folic acid is part of supportive care in thalassemia and does not raise fetal hemoglobin. Tell: the drug that reduces vaso-occlusive events is hydroxyurea.

Correct. Disease modification in sickle cell disease is hydroxyurea, which raises fetal hemoglobin and reduces vaso-occlusive events. Her repeated crises are exactly what it is used to reduce; fetal hemoglobin of 10 to 20 percent lessens clinical severity.
Penicillin prophylaxis is childhood prevention against encapsulated bacteria. Tell: her problem is recurrent vaso-occlusion, which the fetal hemoglobin-raising drug reduces.

set2.q: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell disease is admitted for a pain crisis. On day 2 he develops fever, chest pain, shortness of breath and hypoxemia, and his chest radiograph shows a new pulmonary infiltrate. Which complication does this represent?
opts: Correct. Acute chest syndrome should be considered in sickle cell disease with chest pain, fever, shortness of breath, hypoxemia and pulmonary infiltrates on a chest radiograph. It is often associated with an acute pain event, is the leading cause of death in sickle cell disease and carries more than 10 percent mortality in adults.
Splenic infarct is a sickle cell infarction, but it does not produce hypoxemia and a lung infiltrate. Tell: chest pain, fever, hypoxemia and a new infiltrate define the chest complication.
Aseptic necrosis of the femoral head causes joint pain, not fever with hypoxemia and an infiltrate. Tell: his findings are in the lungs.

A pain crisis brings pain, tenderness, anxiety and tachycardia, but not new hypoxemia with a pulmonary infiltrate. Tell: an infiltrate during a pain event means the crisis has become acute chest syndrome.

set2.q: A 22-year-old man has 3 weeks of fatigue, two recent bacterial infections, gum bleeding and petechiae. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL), white blood cell count 1,600 cells per microliter (normal 4,500-11,000), platelets 18,000 per microliter (normal 150,000-450,000) and the reticulocyte count is low. The smear shows no hypersegmented neutrophils, and B12 and folate levels are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Folate deficiency causes a megaloblastic anemia with macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Tell: his folate is normal and his smear lacks the megaloblastic changes; his picture is all three lines failing.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. He has pancytopenia, loss of all three cell lines, with recurrent infections from neutropenia, bleeding and petechiae from thrombocytopenia, and fatigue from anemia. Loss of hematopoietic stem cells defines aplastic anemia, and half of cases occur in the first three decades, with a small peak between ages 20 and 25.

B12 deficiency is a megaloblastic anemia that can affect other myeloid lines to a lesser degree, with neurologic findings as its distinguishing feature. Tell: his B12 is normal and his smear has no hypersegmented neutrophils.
ruled out by a stated finding

Anemia of chronic kidney disease lowers the red cell line through low erythropoietin and is almost universal in dialysis patients. Tell: nothing in his history points to kidney disease, and his white cells and platelets are low too.

opts: Fava beans are a listed trigger and his own attack came from them; the treatment message is simply do not eat them. Tell: avoiding the trigger is the core of his care.

Correct. Education for this deficiency is to avoid oxidative triggers and seek care for jaundice or dark urine, the signs of an acute hemolytic attack. With trigger avoidance the prognosis is usually favorable.
Nothing in his history suggests iron deficiency, so daily iron tablets are not part of his education. Tell: his education centers on avoiding oxidant triggers and recognizing jaundice or dark urine.
Splenectomy is possible only for recurrent attacks, and he has had one. Tell: one attack calls for trigger avoidance and education, not surgery.

set2.q: A 16-year-old boy with severe beta thalassemia has received frequent red cell transfusions for years. He now has fatigue and a rising ferritin. Which complication of his disease and its treatment is most concerning?
opts: Correct. Iron overload is part of the clinical course of thalassemia, and transfusion, used only when absolutely necessary, can exacerbate it. His years of transfusions and rising ferritin point to iron loading, which calls for iron monitoring in follow-up.
Iron deficiency would lower the ferritin, while his is rising after repeated transfusions. Tell: transfused iron accumulates, so the risk is overload.
Thalassemia is Coombs negative, and nothing in his story describes an antibody process. Tell: the named transfusion risk in thalassemia is iron overload.
Folic acid is part of supportive care, and excess folate is not a listed concern. Tell: the complication tied to transfusion is iron overload.

set2.q: A 62-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has fatigue. Her hemoglobin is 10.4 g/dL (normal 12.0-15.5 g/dL), mean corpuscular volume 82 fL (normal 80-100 fL), ferritin 310 ng/mL (normal 15-200 ng/mL), total iron-binding capacity 210 mcg/dL (normal 250-450 mcg/dL), transferrin saturation 12% (normal 20-50%) and reticulocyte count 0.4% (normal 0.5-2.5%). Which anemia do these results fit?
opts: Nothing in her history or panel points to sideroblastic anemia; her saturation is low at 12% alongside a long-standing inflammatory disease. Tell: a low saturation with an inflammatory disease points to chronic disease.
ruled out by a stated finding
Her panel shows no iron deficiency pattern: the total iron-binding capacity is decreased at 210 mcg/dL, the chronic disease pattern. Tell: iron deficiency raises the binding capacity.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory condition, and her panel fits anemia of chronic disease: a mild anemia, normal mean corpuscular volume, ferritin normal or increased (310 ng/mL), total iron-binding capacity decreased (210 mcg/dL), low transferrin saturation and a reticulocyte count that is usually low.
Iron deficiency has an increased total iron-binding capacity; hers is decreased at 210 mcg/dL. Tell: a decreased binding capacity with an inflammatory disease points to chronic disease.

opts: Hematology for a bone marrow biopsy and smear

Hematology is for iron deficiency whose diagnosis is not confirmed or that does not respond to oral iron. His diagnosis is clear and a bleeding source must be found first. Tell: a positive stool test sends him to the gut specialist.
Cardiology for an echocardiogram before iron

Cardiology is consulted when an anticoagulant may need to stop in severe iron deficiency; no anticoagulant is mentioned, and the stool test points to the gut. Tell: the urgent question is the bleeding source, which colonoscopy and endoscopy answer.
ruled out by a stated finding
Dietitian for a high-iron diet before more tests

Diet is not the issue when blood is found in the stool; chronic blood loss is the most common cause of iron deficiency in adults. Tell: a positive guaiac test needs colonoscopy and endoscopy, not diet advice.

Correct. His microcytic anemia and low ferritin are iron deficiency, and the positive stool guaiac test points to gastrointestinal blood loss. A gastrointestinal bleed calls for a gastrointestinal consult for colonoscopy and endoscopy to evaluate for colorectal cancer, while the cause is treated and iron replaced.

opts: Her mild anemia comes from lead, not iron loss, and iron does not stop the exposure. Tell: the first step is removing her from the source of lead.

Correct. Treatment of lead poisoning starts with stopping exposure, and further treatment is based on the lead level. Chelating agents are kept for severe cases with neurologic effects, which she does not have.
Succimer is used in severe cases with neurologic effects; her symptoms are mild and abdominal only. Tell: removing the exposure comes first, and chelation waits for severity.
Dimercaprol is another chelating agent for severe, neurologic lead poisoning; she has mild colic and no neurologic signs. Tell: mild cases begin by ending the exposure.

His B12 level is 230 pg/mL (normal 200-900 pg/mL), at the borderline, and his folate level is normal. Clinical suspicion of B12 deficiency continues. Which test should be ordered next?
opts: Correct. B12 and folate levels are the initial tests but are not very sensitive, and his B12 is borderline while suspicion continues. Methylmalonic acid rises with B12 deficiency but not with folate deficiency, because its conversion to succinyl CoA requires only B12, so it settles the question.

Anti-parietal cell antibodies may be present in pernicious anemia but are neither sensitive nor specific, and they come after B12 deficiency is established. Tell: first confirm the deficiency with methylmalonic acid, then look for its cause.

A bone marrow biopsy is required to diagnose aplastic anemia, which presents with pancytopenia. Tell: a borderline B12 level in a macrocytic anemia is clarified by a blood metabolite, methylmalonic acid, not by sampling the marrow.
Ferritin and transferrin saturation belong to the microcytic anemia workup. Tell: his cells are large, so the iron panel does not answer whether he is B12 deficient; methylmalonic acid does.

opts: Transfusion can exacerbate iron overload in thalassemia, so more of it worsens the problem. Tell: overload with phlebotomy unsuitable is treated with chelation.

Correct. Secondary iron overload is managed by treating the cause and considering chelation when phlebotomy is unsuitable. A patient who still needs transfusion for anemia cannot have blood removed, so chelation is the option.
Phlebotomy is the treatment of primary hemochromatosis, but removing blood from a transfusion-dependent anemic patient is unsuitable. Tell: when phlebotomy cannot be used, chelation is considered.
ruled out by a stated finding
Glucocorticoids are the initial treatment of autoimmune hemolytic anemia and do not remove iron. Tell: his problem is transfused iron, removed by chelation.

set2.q: A 42-year-old man with lead poisoning from refinishing old painted furniture has been removed from the exposure. He has confusion, irritability and peripheral neuropathy, a severely elevated blood lead level, a hemoglobin of 10.9 g/dL (normal 13.5-17.5 g/dL) and basophilic stippling (an abnormal collection of nucleic acids in the cells) on his smear. Which treatment is indicated now?
opts: His microcytic anemia comes from lead, not iron depletion, and iron does nothing for the neurologic damage. Tell: severe neurologic lead poisoning calls for a chelating agent.
Pyridoxine occasionally helps sideroblastic anemia; it does not remove lead. Tell: with severe neurologic effects the treatment is chelation.
Epoetin alfa supports red cell production in anemia of chronic disease with a hemoglobin below 10 g/dL; it neither removes lead nor treats neurologic toxicity. Tell: remove the metal with succimer.

Correct. Lead poisoning is treated by stopping exposure and according to the lead level; in severe cases with neurologic effects, chelating agents can be used: succimer, dimercaprol or ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid. He is already removed from the source and has severe neurologic involvement.

opts: Her reticulocytes are high, so the marrow is already responding; a marrow biopsy is not part of the hemolysis workup. Tell: the hallmark of hemolysis is seen in circulating blood, on the smear.

Hemoglobin electrophoresis is not among the listed hemolysis tests (complete blood count, reticulocytes, bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, urinalysis, smear). Tell: the first look for hemolysis is the smear for fragments; electrophoresis answers a narrower question.

A liver biopsy is not part of the hemolysis workup; her jaundice and high reticulocytes call for blood tests and a smear review. Tell: suspected hemolysis is worked up with blood tests and a smear, not a liver biopsy.

Correct. A peripheral blood smear should be ordered on a patient with suspected hemolytic anemia; the hallmark finding of hemolysis is schistocytes, red blood cell fragments. It belongs to the workup with a complete blood count, reticulocytes, bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin and urinalysis.

opts: Correct. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism, so remember venous thromboembolism prophylaxis for inpatients, and consider it in outpatients. As an inpatient with this disease he should have it ordered.

Splenectomy is among the other options after glucocorticoids and rituximab, not an admission step for a stable patient just started on steroids. Tell: the inpatient order flagged for this disease is clot prevention.
Hemolysis retains the products of red cell destruction, including iron, so nothing here suggests iron deficiency. Tell: the important note for this disease is its venous clot risk.
Immediate stabilization is for a hemoglobin below 6 g/dL, a rapid decline or instability. Tell: he is stable at 8.1 g/dL, so the standing need is thromboembolism prophylaxis.
ruled out by a stated finding

opts: Referral for an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent belongs to anemia of chronic kidney disease. Tell: in iron deficiency, find the loss and reinforce iron use.
Seek the loss; refer if needed

Correct. Follow-up of iron deficiency is to identify blood loss, reinforce iron use and refer to gastrointestinal specialists if indicated. With the cause and iron stores corrected, it usually resolves.
Urgent hematology with infection and bleeding precautions is the aplastic anemia row. Tell: iron deficiency follow-up hunts the source of blood loss.
Monitoring neurologic recovery belongs to megaloblastic anemia after B12 or folate treatment. Tell: iron deficiency needs the blood loss found.

set2.q: A 45-year-old woman has a white blood cell count of 2,400 cells per microliter (normal 4,500-11,000). Her differential shows neutrophils 30% (normal 40-70%), bands 5% (normal 0-5%), lymphocytes 55% and monocytes 10%. How is her neutropenia classified?
opts: A white count of 2,400 with 35% neutrophils plus bands gives 840, well under the 1,500 top of the mild range. Tell: a low total white count with this differential is clearly neutropenic.
Mild neutropenia is 1,000-1,500 cells per microliter, and her count works out to 2,400 x 35% = 840. Tell: below 1,000 the grade drops to moderate.

Correct. Absolute neutrophil count = white count x (neutrophils + bands)% / 100 = 2,400 x 35 / 100 = 840 cells per microliter. Moderate neutropenia is 500-999, mild is 1,000-1,500 and severe is below 500.
Severe neutropenia is below 500 cells per microliter; even neutrophils alone give 2,400 x 30% = 720. Tell: adding the bands makes 840, inside the moderate range of 500-999.

set2.q: A 21-year-old woman has aplastic anemia confirmed by bone marrow biopsy. Her sister is a suitable donor. Which treatment is indicated?
opts: An erythropoiesis-stimulating agent is considered for anemia of chronic kidney disease, where erythropoietin is low. Tell: her marrow has lost its stem cells, so there is nothing for the agent to stimulate.
Folic acid treats folate deficiency, a megaloblastic anemia. Tell: aplastic anemia is not a vitamin shortage, and with a suitable donor its treatment is transplant.
Watching counts suits transient viral leukopenia, which often resolves. Tell: untreated aplastic anemia kills most patients within a year, so she needs transplant, not observation.

Correct. The treatment of aplastic anemia is bone marrow transplant, and five-year survival is above 75% for patients transplanted from a suitable donor, as her sister is. Most untreated patients die within one year from disease-related complications.
